title: New Spark risk parameters do not break existing loans — non-conforming positions are recalled at the earliest permitted date
content:
A.6.1.1.1.3.7.2.5.4 and A.6.1.1.1.3.8.2.5.4 use identical wording: Spark may update approved assets, risk parameters and program details via governance, and "if a previously issued loan no longer conforms with Spark's current operational mandate due to a non-emergency parameter update, Spark will recall the loan at the earliest possible opportunity, **while respecting the agreed loan duration**."

The final clause resolves a conflict that any live mandate eventually faces. Governance must be able to tighten policy — otherwise the first bad asset approval is permanent. But a governance vote cannot rewrite a signed loan agreement, and pretending otherwise would make Spark an unreliable counterparty that no institutional borrower could underwrite.

The resolution is grandfathering with a mandatory exit. The new policy binds immediately for new business; existing positions run to their contractual maturity and are then not renewed. "Earliest possible opportunity" plus "respecting the duration" means the recall lands at the first date Spark is contractually entitled to demand it — which for the evergreen and demand structures Spark prefers is essentially immediately, and for a fixed term is at expiry.

This is also the strongest argument for the short tenors elsewhere in these sections. A one-month Arkis maximum and a six-month offchain maximum are the upper bounds on how long a governance decision can be blocked by a pre-existing contract. The tenor limit is not only interest-rate risk management; it is the mechanism that keeps the mandate enforceable within a governance cycle.

The obligation is stated as a duty on Spark rather than a permission, so a contributor cannot elect to keep a profitable non-conforming loan running on the grounds that it is still performing.
description: Governance may tighten approved assets and parameters at will, but a loan rendered non-conforming is recalled 'while respecting the agreed loan duration', so contracts survive policy change.
